title.narrative: Diakonia Democratic Local Governance phase II
Diakonia Democratic Local Governance phase II

description.narrative: Diakonia har sedan 2018 fått stöd för insatsen "Enhancing Citizen Participation in Local Governance in Zimbabwe", som syftar till att på olika sätt stärka lokal demokrati i landet genom ökat deltagande, stärkt insyn och en förbättrad dialog mellan ansvarstagare och rättighetsbärare. Insatsen har haft ett särskilt fokus på ungdomars och kvinnors deltagande. I den andra fasen har fokus på kvinnor och ungdomar stärkts ytterligare och tanken är att man skall genomföra aktiviteter i såväl nya som gamla kommuner, där de man arbetat i sedan tidigare skall fungera som en modell för de nya kommunerna. Tre partnerorganisationer fasas ut och två nya tillkommer. Utifrån erfarenheter från första fasen skall mer stöd ges till ansvarstagare, då både utvärdering och andra inblandade parter uppmärksammade en obalans där ansvarstagares kapacitet inte utvecklades i takt med rättighetsbärarna och de krav som började ställas efter utbildningar.

The development objective of the programme is "Enhanced democratic governance contributing to improved living conditions for citizens in Zimbabwe." The overall programme objective is formulated as follows: "Rights holders enjoying their rights to quality and gender responsive social services from transparent and accountable local authorities."
The programme is a follow-on proposal to the ongoing programme "Enhancing Citizen Participation in Local Governance in Zimbabwe, 2018-2022". In this new phase, focus on women and youth will be further strengthened, with a more balanced approach of support to both duty bearers and rights holders. Another area of increased focus is the cooperation within and between Consortium members.

The development objective of the project:
Enhanced democratic governance contributing to improved living conditions for citizens in Zimbabwe.
Overall Programme Objective:
Rights holders, particularly women, youth and other vulnerable and marginalized groups realize and enjoy their rights to quality and gender responsive social services from transparent and accountable local authorities.
Programme Outcomes:
1) By December 2025, there is increased meaningful participation of rights holders (women, and youth) in selected rural and urban areas.
2) By December 2025, there is enhanced responsiveness, transparency and accountability of local government systems and structures in selected rural and urban local authorities.
3) By December 2025, Civil Society organisations in the programme have strengthened institutional and technical capacity and have developed collaborative platforms for learning and sharing best practices.
Theory of Change:
Outcome 1: We believe that if women and youth are not just represented in local government structures, but are meaningfully contributing, and are financially included through economic empowerment, then they will be able to positively influence local governance and push for quality service delivery.
Outcome 2: if local authorities have trained leaders and staff that have adequately designed and followed mandates and competencies, then accountability and transparency is attainable. Armed with sufficient political will and sufficient capacity, the local authorities leadership and staff should be able to steer the positive transformation of the local government systems and processes in a manner that is inclusive of women and youth.
Outcome 3: if Diakonia works with partners to strengthen their coherence, networking and programme coordination in the context of a one programme approach (in particular with regard to integrating women and youth empowerment taking advantage of digital technology), then they will be better able to contribute to transparent and accountable local authorities that serve the needs of youth and women, driving the processes of positive change and inclusivity.

Despite the success scored during the year, the project in Zimbabwe navigated a complex and evolving landscape marked by economic instability, political tightening, and regulatory shifts. The Diakonia civic engagement project nonetheless achieved transformative progress in promoting inclusive governance, citizen participation, and institutional accountability, even as civic space shrank, particularly following the enactment of the Private Voluntary Organisations (PVO) Amendment Act.
Citizen outreach exceeded expectations, engaging 18,643 individuals, 10,849 women and 7,794 men, surpassing the initial target of 16,000. This led to increased civic action, such as youth in Gwanda joining development committees and communities in Victoria Falls influencing budget allocations for roads, education, and water management, demonstrating a shift from passive citizenship to active civic engagement.
Civic platform access surged, with 116,231 individuals participating far beyond the target of 7,000. This rise in engagement fostered stronger dialogue between citizens and duty bearers, contributing to a more responsive governance environment. Additionally, 54,210 citizens were trained in service delivery monitoring, resulting in tangible improvements like the opening of a maternal shelter in Shamva and better clinic staffing in Gokwe.
Leadership development efforts empowered 2,373 women and youth, significantly exceeding the target of 200. This led to increased advocacy and participation in governance processes. In parallel, 1,030 local officials received training, which improved collaboration and transparency between communities and authorities.
Policy and program support expanded, with 76 women and youth focused initiatives implemented. These included youth centers, women's markets, and recreational facility refurbishments, which enhanced local infrastructure and economic opportunities. Transparency was boosted through the public sharing of 56 key documents, while media training led to 30 published articles and 11 position papers amplifying citizen voices and influencing policy discourse.
Research and advocacy flourished, producing 20 reports and position papers more than triple the target. Notably, We Lead Trusts Shadow Bill proposed reforms for youth access to education and mental health support. Seven joint advocacy statements and 17 public interest issues presented to duty bearers led to increased budget allocations for disability inclusion and legal aid sessions.
Innovation drove impact, with the launch of the Gender Responsive Social Services Delivery (GRSSD) mobile app in Bindura improving access to essential services for women and girls. Legislative lobbying also succeeded in harmonizing age of consent and marriage laws, advancing child protection.
Gender mainstreaming was embedded throughout the program, ensuring inclusive participation and accessibility. Activities were scheduled with gender roles in mind, venues were adapted for persons with disabilities, and sex-dis-aggregated data collection informed strategy adjustments. Local authorities received training in gender-responsive budgeting, and traditional leaders were sensitized on gender equity, shifting community norms and increasing acceptance of women and youth in decision-making spaces.
Collaboration among implementing partners was significantly strengthened, leading to more coordinated efforts, shared learning, and unified advocacy. This enhanced synergy improved program coherence and amplified the collective impact of civic engagement activities across regions.
Despite these achievements, the project faced escalating challenges. Bureaucratic delays in securing MOUs, often due to inconsistent procedures and reluctance from officials to support politically sensitive activities, slowed implementation and limited the reach of advocacy efforts. Government clearance requirements added further delays and scrutiny, particularly affecting community engagement components.
Civic space was restricted during the SADC Summit, disrupting public gatherings and outreach activities. This led to reduced visibility and momentum for civic initiatives during a critical period.
Economic instability, triggered by the introduction of the Zimbabwe Gold currency, complicated budgeting and procurement due to exchange rate fluctuations. This created financial unpredictability for implementing partners and affected timely delivery of services.
The PVO Amendment Act imposed severe restrictions on civil society organizations. It expanded surveillance, limited lobbying, and empowered authorities to suspend or dissolve organizations. These measures undermined CSO autonomy and fostered fear and self-censorship, threatening the sustainability and long-term impact of civic engagement efforts.
Reputational risks emerged, with unverified allegations against a partner organization drawing politically motivated scrutiny. This highlighted the vulnerability of CSOs and underscored the need for robust accountability mechanisms to maintain trust and legitimacy.
Donor funding declined, as global priorities shifted. This reduced financial support for development initiatives in Zimbabwe, posing risks to the continuity and scale of programming.
Amid these pressures, Diakonia initiated a major internal restructuring aimed at improving efficiency and strategic alignment. However, the process, which involved closure of some country offices and changes in reporting structures introduced potential transitional challenges that could temporarily hinder the organizations ability to effectively monitor, implement, and follow up on program activities.
By late 2024, the programme had brought about meaningful and far-reaching change. Citizens changed from passive recipients of services to active participants in governance. Despite civic space tightening, economic volatility, funding constraints, and computational risks, the combination of empowered communities, responsive institutions, strengthened partnerships, and innovative tools fostered a culture of civic participation, accountability, and inclusive governance laying a strong foundation for sustainable democratic change.
